title: Tropical Storm Krovahn may not re-enter PAR but continues to enhance ‘habagat’
summary: The tropical storm with the international name “Krovahn” now has only a slim chance of re-entering the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR), but it will continue to enhance the southwest monsoon…

blocks.text: The tropical storm with the international name “Krovahn” now has only a slim chance of re-entering the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR), but it will continue to enhance the southwest monsoon or “habagat” and bring more rain over parts of Luzon, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said on Monday, Sept. 7. PAGASA weather specialist Aldczar Aurelio said Krovahn, formerly called “Pilandok,” was located 1,155 kilometers east-northeast of extreme Northern Luzon as of 3 a.m. Monday, moving eastward at 10 kilometers per hour. Krovahn exited the PAR on Sept. 3. Over the next 24 hours, occasional heavy rains may persist over Zambales, Bataan, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro due to the enhanced habagat. Metro Manila, Ilocos Region, Abra, Benguet, Antique, and the rest of Central Luzon, Calabarzon, and Mimaropa may experience cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms. The rest of the country may have partly cloudy skies with chances of isolated rain showers or thunderstorms. Meanwhile, Ambuklao and Binga dams in Benguet and San Roque Dam in Pangasinan continued to spill excess water, based on PAGASA’s monitoring. As of 8 a.m. Monday, two gates of Ambuklao Dam were open. Its water level was at 751.41 meters, just 0.59 meter below its 752-meter normal high water level. Binga Dam’s water level was at 573.9 meters, or 1.1 meters below its 575-meter normal high water level. Two of its gates remained open. San Roque Dam was at 279.46 meters, just 0.54 meter below its normal high water level, although this was lower than the 282.08 meters recorded the previous day. Two of its gates also remained open. The three dams form part of a cascading system, with water released from Ambuklao mostly flowing into Binga Dam before Binga’s releases move downstream to San Roque Dam.
